smt-2022-power-2-1a.title: Count the flips
smt-2022-power-2-1a.body: $X=x$ happens exactly when the first $x-1$ flips are tails and flip $x$ is heads. The flips are independent, and tails has probability $1-p$ and heads $p$, so the probability is $(1-p)^{x-1}\cdot p$. ∎

smt-2022-power-2-1b.title: Count the configurations
smt-2022-power-2-1b.body: $X=x$ means exactly $x$ of the $n$ flips are heads. There are $\binom nx$ ways to choose which flips are heads. For each such choice, independence gives probability $p^x(1-p)^{n-x}$. The choices are mutually exclusive events, so their probabilities add: $\binom nxp^x(1-p)^{n-x}$. ∎

smt-2022-power-2-2.title: Differentiate under the integral
smt-2022-power-2-2.body: $\widetilde X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{sx}p_X(x)\,dx$. Differentiating $k$ times with respect to $s$ (allowed by assumption) gives $\widetilde X^{(k)}(s)=\int x^ke^{sx}p_X(x)\,dx$, since $\frac{d^k}{ds^k}e^{sx}=x^ke^{sx}$. At $s=0$ this is $\int x^kp_X(x)\,dx=\mathbb E[X^k]$. For a variable on the nonnegative integers the same argument works with $\sum_n n^ke^{sn}p_X(n)$. ∎

smt-2022-power-2-3a.title: Condition on the first flip
smt-2022-power-2-3a.body:
With probability $p$ the first flip is heads and $X=1$. Otherwise ($1-p$) one flip is used and, by independence, the number of further flips has the same distribution as $X$. So $\mathbb E[X]=p\cdot1+(1-p)(1+\mathbb E[X])$, giving $p\,\mathbb E[X]=1$ and $\mathbb E[X]=\frac1p$ (the expectation is finite since $\sum_xx(1-p)^{x-1}p<\infty$).

**Answer: $\frac1p$**

smt-2022-power-2-3b.title: Indicator variables and the binomial theorem
smt-2022-power-2-3b.body:
Write $X=I_1+\cdots+I_n$ with $I_j$ the indicator that flip $j$ is heads; $I_j$ are independent, with $\mathbb E[I_j]=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(I_j)=\mathbb E[I_j^2]-p^2=p-p^2=p(1-p)$.

By linearity, $\mathbb E[X]=np$; by independence, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)$.

For the $z$-transform: $\widehat X(z)=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom nizi\,p^i(1-p)^{n-i}=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom ni(zp)^i(1-p)^{n-i}=(1-p+zp)^n$ by the binomial theorem. ∎

smt-2022-power-2-3c.title: Use the $z$-transform
smt-2022-power-2-3c.body:
$\widehat X(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}z^ke^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}=e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda z}=e^{\lambda(z-1)}$ (Taylor series of $e^{\lambda z}$).

Since $\widehat X'(z)=\mathbb E[Xz^{X-1}]$ and $\widehat X''(z)=\mathbb E[X(X-1)z^{X-2}]$, we get $\mathbb E[X]=\widehat X'(1)=\lambda e^{0}=\lambda$ and $\mathbb E[X(X-1)]=\widehat X''(1)=\lambda^2$. Hence $\mathbb E[X^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda^2+\lambda-\lambda^2=\lambda$. (Equivalently, from $\widetilde X(s)=e^{\lambda(e^s-1)}$: $\widetilde X'(0)=\lambda$, $\widetilde X''(0)=\lambda(1+\lambda)$.) ∎

smt-2022-power-2-4.title: Heuristic
smt-2022-power-2-4.body: Split the hour into $n$ tiny time steps of length $\frac1n$. In each step an arrival (a head) occurs with probability $\frac\lambda n$, independently of what happened in other steps, so the expected number of arrivals is $n\cdot\frac\lambda n=\lambda$. As $n\to\infty$ the steps become infinitesimal: arrivals at any instant are independent of the past and occur at rate $\lambda$ per hour, which is precisely the defining property of Poisson arrivals. So $X_n$ should converge to $Y$ (this is made precise in Problem 2.6).

smt-2022-power-2-5.title: Differentiate the power series
smt-2022-power-2-5.body:
$\widehat X(z)=\sum_{i\ge0}z^ip_X(i)$. Differentiating $k$ times, $\widehat X^{(k)}(z)=\sum_{i\ge k}i(i-1)\cdots(i-k+1)z^{i-k}p_X(i)=k!\,p_X(k)+\sum_{i>k}i(i-1)\cdots(i-k+1)z^{i-k}p_X(i)$. At $z=0$ all terms with $i>k$ vanish, so $\widehat X^{(k)}(0)=k!\,p_X(k)$, i.e. $p_X(k)=\frac{1}{k!}\widehat X^{(k)}(0)$.

(Consequently the $z$-transform determines the distribution.) ∎

smt-2022-power-2-6.title: Take the limit
smt-2022-power-2-6.body: With $p=\frac\lambda n$: $\widehat{X_n}(z)=\left(1-\frac\lambda n+\frac{\lambda z}n\right)^n=\left(1+\frac{\lambda(z-1)}{n}\right)^n$. Since $\left(1+\frac cn\right)^n\to e^c$ for every real $c$, taking $c=\lambda(z-1)$ gives $\lim_{n\to\infty}\widehat{X_n}(z)=e^{\lambda(z-1)}=\widehat Y(z)$. By Problem 2.5 the probabilities $p(k)=\frac1{k!}\widehat{\cdot}^{(k)}(0)$ are determined by the $z$-transform, so the limit distribution of $X_n$ is $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$. ∎

smt-2022-power-2-7.title: No arrivals in $[0,t]$
smt-2022-power-2-7.body:
Start the process at an arrival (time $0$). The time $X$ until the next arrival exceeds $t$ exactly when there are no arrivals in $(0,t]$. The number of arrivals in that interval is $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda t)$, so $P[X>t]=P[\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda t)=0]=e^{-\lambda t}\frac{(\lambda t)^0}{0!}=e^{-\lambda t}$.

Then $P[X>t]=\int_t^\infty p_X(x)\,dx$; differentiating, $-p_X(t)=\frac{d}{dt}e^{-\lambda t}=-\lambda e^{-\lambda t}$ (fundamental theorem of calculus), so $p_X(t)=\lambda e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$, i.e. $X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$. The same argument applies to any inter-arrival time. ∎

smt-2022-power-2-8a.title: Integrate by parts
smt-2022-power-2-8a.body: $\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty x\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx=\left[-xe^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^\infty+\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda x}dx=0+\frac1\lambda=\frac1\lambda$.

smt-2022-power-2-8b.title: Integrate
smt-2022-power-2-8b.body: $\widetilde X(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{sx}\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx=\lambda\int_0^\infty e^{-(\lambda-s)x}dx=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-s}$ for $s<\lambda$. (Check: $\widetilde X'(0)=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda^2}=\frac1\lambda=\mathbb E[X]$.)

smt-2022-power-2-8c.title: Condition on $X$
smt-2022-power-2-8c.body: $P[X<Y]=\int_0^\infty P[Y>t]\,\lambda e^{-\lambda t}dt=\int_0^\infty e^{-\mu t}\lambda e^{-\lambda t}dt=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}$.

smt-2022-power-3-1a.title: Waiting for everyone ahead
smt-2022-power-3-1a.body: An arriving customer sees the steady-state number $N$ of people in the system (arrivals are Poisson, so they see time averages, as proved in Problem 3.4). By memorylessness of the $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu)$ service times, each of those $N$ people, including the one currently in service, needs expected time $\frac1\mu$ more, and service times are independent of $N$. So the expected wait before service starts is $\frac{\mathbb E[N]}{\mu}$; then the customer's own service takes $\frac1\mu$. Hence $\mathbb E[T]=\frac{\mathbb E[N]+1}{\mu}$.

smt-2022-power-3-1b.title: Steady-state distribution
smt-2022-power-3-1b.body:
Let $\pi_i$ be the steady-state probability of $i$ people in the system. Consider the cut between states $i$ and $i+1$: the system moves up across it at rate $\lambda\pi_i$ (arrivals while in state $i$) and down across it at rate $\mu\pi_{i+1}$ (a service completion in state $i+1$). Since up-crossings and down-crossings alternate, over a long time they occur equally often, so $\lambda\pi_i=\mu\pi_{i+1}$, i.e. $\pi_{i+1}=\rho\pi_i$ and $\pi_i=\rho^i\pi_0$.

Normalising, $1=\pi_0\sum_{i\ge0}\rho^i=\frac{\pi_0}{1-\rho}$, so $\pi_i=(1-\rho)\rho^i$. Then $\mathbb E[N]=\sum_{i\ge0}i(1-\rho)\rho^i=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu-\lambda}$.

By part (a), $\mathbb E[T]=\frac{\mathbb E[N]+1}\mu=\frac1\mu\cdot\frac1{1-\rho}=\frac1{\mu-\lambda}$. ∎

smt-2022-power-3-2a.title: Definitions
smt-2022-power-3-2a.body: The average number of jobs in the system over $[0,t]$ is $\frac1t\int_0^tN(t')\,dt'$, so $\overline N=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t\int_0^tN(t')\,dt'$. The average time in the system of the first $A(t)$ jobs to arrive is $\frac1{A(t)}\sum_{i=1}^{A(t)}T_i$, so $\overline T=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1{A(t)}\sum_{i=1}^{A(t)}T_i$ (also equal to the limit along $C(t)$, as both $A(t),C(t)\to\infty$ at the same rate).

smt-2022-power-3-2b.title: Squeeze the integral
smt-2022-power-3-2b.body:
The integral $\int_0^tN(t')\,dt'$ is the total time that jobs have spent in the system by time $t$: each job contributes the length of the part of its stay that lies inside $[0,t]$. A job that has already left by time $t$ contributes its full $T_i$; any job that has arrived by time $t$ contributes at most $T_i$. Writing $\mathcal D(t)$ for the set of jobs that have left by time $t$ ($|\mathcal D(t)|=C(t)$) and $\mathcal A(t)$ for those that have arrived ($|\mathcal A(t)|=A(t)$): $$\sum_{i\in\mathcal D(t)}T_i\le\int_0^tN(t')\,dt'\le\sum_{i\in\mathcal A(t)}T_i.$$

Divide by $t$: $\frac1t\sum_{i\in\mathcal D(t)}T_i=\frac{C(t)}t\cdot\frac1{C(t)}\sum_{i\in\mathcal D(t)}T_i\to\lambda\overline T$ and $\frac1t\sum_{i\in\mathcal A(t)}T_i=\frac{A(t)}t\cdot\frac1{A(t)}\sum_{i\in\mathcal A(t)}T_i\to\lambda\overline T$ (in a system with a steady state both averages of the $T_i$ converge to the same $\overline T$). By the squeeze theorem $\frac1t\int_0^tN\to\lambda\overline T$, i.e. $\overline N=\lambda\overline T$. With Theorem 3.2 ($\overline N=\mathbb E[N]$, $\overline T=\mathbb E[T]$) this gives $\mathbb E[N]=\lambda\mathbb E[T]$. ∎

smt-2022-power-3-3.title: Solve two equations
smt-2022-power-3-3.body: Substituting $\mathbb E[T]=\mathbb E[N]/\lambda$ into $\mathbb E[T]=\frac{\mathbb E[N]+1}\mu$ gives $\frac{\mathbb E[N]}\lambda=\frac{\mathbb E[N]+1}{\mu}$, so $\mu\mathbb E[N]=\lambda\mathbb E[N]+\lambda$ and $\mathbb E[N]=\frac\lambda{\mu-\lambda}$. Then $\mathbb E[T]=\frac{\mathbb E[N]}{\lambda}=\frac1{\mu-\lambda}$.

smt-2022-power-3-4.title: Independence from the past
smt-2022-power-3-4.body:
Let $E(t,\delta)$ be the event that an arrival occurs in $[t,t+\delta]$. The system state $N(t)$ is determined by arrivals and service up to time $t$. For a Poisson process the arrivals in $[t,t+\delta]$ are independent of everything that happened before $t$ (memorylessness of the exponential inter-arrival time: no matter when the last arrival before $t$ occurred, the time to the next one is again $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$). Hence $E(t,\delta)$ is independent of $\{N(t)=n\}$, so $P[N(t)=n\mid E(t,\delta)]=P[N(t)=n]$.

Taking $\delta\to0$ and then $t\to\infty$: $a_n=\lim_{t\to\infty}\lim_{\delta\to0}P[N(t)=n\mid E(t,\delta)]=\lim_{t\to\infty}P[N(t)=n]=\pi_n$. ∎

smt-2022-power-3-5.title: Birth-death balance
smt-2022-power-3-5.body:
Let the state be the number $j\in\{0,\dots,k\}$ of busy servers and $\pi_j$ its steady-state probability. In state $j$ the next service completion happens after $\min$ of $j$ independent $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu)$ times, which is $\mathrm{Exp}(j\mu)$ (since $P[\min>t]=\prod P[X_i>t]=e^{-j\mu t}$), i.e. at total rate $j\mu$; arrivals occur at rate $\lambda$ (and are accepted when $j<k$).

Cut between $j-1$ and $j$ ($1\le j\le k$): up-crossings at rate $\lambda\pi_{j-1}$, down-crossings at rate $j\mu\pi_j$; these balance, so $\pi_j=\frac\rho j\pi_{j-1}$ and $\pi_j=\frac{\rho^j}{j!}\pi_0$. Normalising, $\pi_0=\left(\sum_{i=0}^k\frac{\rho^i}{i!}\right)^{-1}$.

By PASTA an arrival sees the time-average state, so $P_{\text{block}}=\pi_k=\dfrac{\rho^k/k!}{\sum_{i=0}^k\rho^i/i!}$. (Equivalently $P[Z=k\mid Z\le k]$ for $Z\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\rho)$: the Erlang loss formula.) ∎

smt-2022-power-4-1.title: Balance arrivals and departures
smt-2022-power-4-1.body: With no matching, pairs leave only by becoming critical. With $N$ pairs present, departures occur at rate $N$, so in steady state the average departure rate is $\mathbb E[N]$. The arrival rate is $m$, so $\mathbb E[N]=m$. Arrivals are Poisson, so by PASTA (Problem 3.4) a new pair sees the time-average number of pairs, namely $m$. (Equivalently: if $z<m$ the next event is an arrival with probability $\frac m{m+z}>\frac12$, and if $z>m$ a departure with probability $\frac z{m+z}>\frac12$, so the size is pulled towards $m$.) ∎

smt-2022-power-4-2a.title: No two present pairs are linked
smt-2022-power-4-2a.body: Whenever a pair arrives and has any link to a pair already present, greedy matches it at once and both leave. So a pair that stays in the market had no links to anyone present on arrival, and any later pair that links to it is matched on arrival and leaves. Therefore at all times there are $0$ links among the pairs present. In particular a pair that becomes critical has nobody to be matched with, so doing nothing at criticality events loses nothing. ∎

smt-2022-power-4-2b.title: Every critical pair is lost
smt-2022-power-4-2b.body: By part (a) every pair that becomes critical is unmatched. Criticality events occur at rate $N$ when $N$ pairs are present, so the time-average rate of unmatched critical pairs is $C=\mathbb E[N]$ and $L=\frac Cm=\frac{\mathbb E[N]}{m}$.

smt-2022-power-4-2c.title: Complement
smt-2022-power-4-2c.body: The new pair fails to be linked to any of the $z$ present pairs with probability $(1-p)^z$ (independent links). So it finds a match with probability $1-(1-p)^z$.

smt-2022-power-4-2d.title: Balance arrival and departure rates
smt-2022-power-4-2d.body: The market grows by $1$ when an arriving pair finds no match, at rate $m(1-p)^z$. It shrinks when an arriving pair is matched (the matched partner leaves, and the arrival itself never joins), at rate $m\left(1-(1-p)^z\right)$, and when a pair becomes critical, at rate $z$. In steady state these balance: $$m(1-p)^z-m\left(1-(1-p)^z\right)-z=0.$$ So $0=2m(1-p)^z-m-z\ge2m(1-pz)-m-z=m-z(2pm+1)=m-z(2d+1)$, using Bernoulli's inequality. Hence $z\ge\frac m{2d+1}$. ∎

smt-2022-power-4-3a.title: Layer-cake formula
smt-2022-power-4-3a.body: For $Y\ge0$ with density $p_Y$, $$\int_0^\infty P[Y>y]\,dy=\int_0^\infty\int_y^\infty p_Y(x)\,dx\,dy=\int_0^\infty p_Y(x)\int_0^x dy\,dx=\int_0^\infty xp_Y(x)\,dx=\mathbb E[Y]$$ (swapping the order of integration; the discrete case is the same). On $[0,k]$ the integrand is a probability, at most $1$, so $\int_0^kP[Y>y]dy\le k$. Therefore $\mathbb E[Y]\le k+\int_k^\infty P[Y>y]\,dy$. ∎

smt-2022-power-4-3b.title: Independent copy
smt-2022-power-4-3b.body:
Let $X'$ be an independent copy of $X$. Since $f$ is increasing and $g$ is decreasing, $f(X)-f(X')$ and $g(X)-g(X')$ have opposite signs (or one is $0$), so $(f(X)-f(X'))(g(X)-g(X'))\le0$ always. Taking expectations and expanding, $$0\ge\mathbb E[f(X)g(X)]-\mathbb E[f(X)g(X')]-\mathbb E[f(X')g(X)]+\mathbb E[f(X')g(X')]=2\mathbb E[f(X)g(X)]-2\mathbb E[f(X)]\mathbb E[g(X)],$$ using independence of $X,X'$ for the cross terms. Hence $\mathbb E[f(X)g(X)]\le\mathbb E[f(X)]\mathbb E[g(X)]$. ∎

(For $X$ uniform on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ this is the rearrangement-inequality statement $\frac1{n}\sum f(i)g(i)\le\frac1{n^2}\sum_i f(i)\sum_jg(j)$.)

smt-2022-power-4-3c.title: Reduce to a bound on $\mathbb E[e^{-dX/m}]$
smt-2022-power-4-3c.body:
Let $a=1-\frac dm$ (positive for large $m$). The function $x\mapsto x$ is increasing and $x\mapsto a^x$ is decreasing, so by 4.3(b), $\mathbb E[Xa^X]\le\mathbb E[X]\,\mathbb E[a^X]$. By $1+x\le e^x$, $a^X\le e^{-dX/m}$. So it suffices to show $\mathbb E\left[e^{-dX/m}\right]\le e^{-d\mathbb E[X]/m}(1+\varepsilon)$ for large $m$.

Let $Y=e^{-\frac dm(X-\mathbb E[X])}$, so we need $\mathbb E[Y]\le1+\varepsilon$. Fix $n=1+\frac\varepsilon2$. For $y\ge n>1$, $Y>y$ means $X-\mathbb E[X]<-\frac{m\ln y}{d}$, so with $k=\frac{\sqrt m\ln y}d$ (so $k\sqrt m=\frac{m\ln y}d$) concentration gives $$P[Y>y]\le c_1\sqrt m\,\exp\left(-c_2\frac{m\ln^2y}{d^2}\right)\le c_1\sqrt m\,y^{-s},\qquad s=\frac{c_2m\ln n}{d^2},$$ using $\ln^2y\ge\ln n\cdot\ln y$ for $y\ge n$. Then by 4.3(a) with $k=n$: $$\mathbb E[Y]\le n+\int_n^\infty c_1\sqrt m\,y^{-s}dy=n+c_1\sqrt m\,\frac{n^{1-s}}{s-1}.$$ As $m\to\infty$, $s\to\infty$ linearly in $m$, so $\sqrt m\,\frac{n^{1-s}}{s-1}\to0$ (an exponentially small factor $n^{-s}$ beats $\sqrt m$). Hence for all large $m$, $\mathbb E[Y]\le n+\frac\varepsilon2=1+\varepsilon$. Combining, $\mathbb E[X(1-\frac dm)^X]\le\mathbb E[X]e^{-d\mathbb E[X]/m}(1+\varepsilon)$. ∎

smt-2022-power-4-4a.title: Links to the other pairs
smt-2022-power-4-4a.body: Under the patient algorithm no matches happen on arrival, so the links form a random graph on the $z$ pairs in which each of the $\binom z2$ potential links is present independently with probability $p$. The critical pair can be matched unless it is linked to none of the other $z-1$ pairs, which has probability $(1-p)^{z-1}$. So it has a match with probability $1-(1-p)^{z-1}$. (If $z$ denotes the number of *other* pairs, this is $1-(1-p)^{z}$; for $p\to0$ the two differ by a factor $1-p\to1$.)

smt-2022-power-4-4b.title: Rate of unmatched critical pairs
smt-2022-power-4-4b.body: With $z$ pairs present, critical pairs occur at rate $z$ and each is unmatched with probability $(1-p)^{z-1}$ (part (a)), so unmatched critical pairs occur at rate $z(1-p)^{z-1}$. Averaging over the steady-state distribution of $N$: $C=\mathbb E\left[N(1-p)^{N-1}\right]$, so $L=\frac1m\mathbb E\left[N(1-p)^{N-1}\right]=\frac{1}{(1-p)m}\mathbb E\left[N(1-p)^N\right]$. Since $p=\frac dm\to0$, this is asymptotically $\frac1m\mathbb E\left[N(1-p)^N\right]=\frac1m\mathbb E\left[N\left(1-\frac dm\right)^N\right]$.

smt-2022-power-4-4c.title: Count departures
smt-2022-power-4-4c.body: In steady state the departure rate equals the arrival rate $m$. Pairs leave only through criticality events: at each such event the critical pair leaves and, if it has a link, one partner leaves with it, so at most $2$ pairs leave per criticality event. Criticality events occur at average rate $\mathbb E[N]$. Therefore $m=\text{departure rate}\le2\mathbb E[N]$, i.e. $\mathbb E[N]\ge\frac m2$. ∎

smt-2022-power-4-4d.title: Monotonicity of $ue^{-du}$
smt-2022-power-4-4d.body: By 4.3(c) (with $\varepsilon\to0$), $L\le\frac1m\mathbb E[N]e^{-d\mathbb E[N]/m}$. Let $u=\frac{\mathbb E[N]}m\ge\frac12$ (Problem 4.4(c)). Then $L\le ue^{-du}$. The function $h(u)=ue^{-du}$ has $h'(u)=e^{-du}(1-du)<0$ for $u>\frac1d$, so for $d\ge2$ it is decreasing on $[\frac12,\infty)$ and $L\le h\left(\tfrac12\right)=\frac12e^{-d/2}$. (The $1+\varepsilon$ factor can be made arbitrarily close to $1$ by taking $m$ large.) Hence $L\le\frac{e^{-d/2}}2$ as $m\to\infty$. ∎

smt-2022-power-5-1.title: Double counting
smt-2022-power-5-1.body: Count pairs $(v,e)$ with $v\in V$, $e\in E$ and $v\in e$. Counting by vertex gives $\sum_v\deg(v)$. Counting by edge, each edge has exactly two endpoints, giving $2|E|$. Hence $\sum_{v\in V}\deg(v)=2|E|$. ∎

smt-2022-power-5-2.title: Check each graph
smt-2022-power-5-2.body:
**Graph 1** (highlighted $\{2\text{-}6,\,1\text{-}5\}$): the uncovered vertices are $3$ and $4$, which are not adjacent, so no edge can be added: maximal. A larger matching exists: $\{1\text{-}4,\,2\text{-}5,\,3\text{-}6\}$ (a perfect matching, size $3$), so it is not maximum.

**Graph 2** (the complete graph on $5$ vertices, highlighted $\{1\text{-}3,\,2\text{-}4\}$): only vertex $5$ is uncovered, so it is maximal; with $5$ vertices a matching has at most $\lfloor5/2\rfloor=2$ edges, so it is also maximum.

**Graph 3** (highlighted $\{1\text{-}4,\,2\text{-}5\}$): vertices $3,6,7$ are uncovered and $3\text{-}7$ and $6\text{-}7$ are edges, so it is not maximal (hence not maximum). Adding $3\text{-}7$ (or $6\text{-}7$) gives a matching of size $3$, which is maximum as $7$ vertices allow at most $3$ edges.

smt-2022-power-5-3.title: Greedy scan
smt-2022-power-5-3.body:
**Algorithm.** Start with $M=\emptyset$. Go through the edges $e=\{u,v\}$ one at a time; if neither $u$ nor $v$ is an endpoint of an edge already in $M$, add $e$ to $M$. Output $M$.

**Correctness.** $M$ is a matching because an edge is only added when both its endpoints are uncovered. It is maximal: if some edge $e\notin M$ could be added, then when $e$ was examined both endpoints were uncovered (a vertex covered later stays covered, and vertices covered earlier were covered when $e$ was examined), contradicting the rule.

**Time.** Each edge needs $2$ endpoint checks, so the checks take $2m$. Each addition costs $1$, and there are at most $m$ of them (indeed at most $|V|/2$), so the total time is at most $2m+m=3m$. Counting only the endpoint checks, $c=2$.

smt-2022-power-5-4.title: Both directions
smt-2022-power-5-4.body:
**($\Rightarrow$)** If there is an augmenting path $P$ for $M$, it has one more non-$M$ edge than $M$ edge (it starts and ends with non-$M$ edges, since its endpoints are uncovered). Swapping the roles of the edges on $P$ (remove $M$-edges of $P$, add the others) gives a matching: internal vertices of $P$ stay covered exactly once, the two endpoints become covered once, and other vertices are unaffected. Its size is $|M|+1$, so $M$ was not maximum.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Suppose $M$ is not maximum; let $M'$ be a larger matching, $|M'|>|M|$. Consider $H=(V,M\triangle M')$. Every vertex has at most one edge from each of $M,M'$, so $H$ has maximum degree $2$ and its components are paths and cycles whose edges alternate between $M$ and $M'$ (cycles are even). Cycles contain equally many edges of each; since $|M'|>|M|$, some component is a path with more $M'$-edges than $M$-edges, i.e. a path that begins and ends with $M'$-edges. Its endpoint $v$ is covered by an $M'$-edge of the path; $v$ is not covered by an $M$-edge, because such an edge would either lie in $H$ (and extend the path) or lie in $M\cap M'$ (and then $v$ would be covered by two edges of $M'$). So both endpoints are uncovered by $M$ and this path is an augmenting path for $M$. ∎

smt-2022-power-5-5a.title: Alternating BFS
smt-2022-power-5-5a.body:
An augmenting path has odd length and starts and ends at uncovered vertices; since $G$ is bipartite its endpoints lie on opposite sides, so it can be written from an uncovered $x\in X$ to an uncovered $y\in Y$, and it alternates: non-$M$ edge $X\to Y$, $M$-edge $Y\to X$, and so on, ending with a non-$M$ edge into $y$.

**Algorithm.** Direct every non-matching edge from $X$ to $Y$ and every matching edge from $Y$ to $X$. Run a breadth-first search in this directed graph started simultaneously from all uncovered vertices of $X$, recording for each visited vertex its parent. If the search reaches an uncovered $y\in Y$, output the path obtained by following parents back to the start. If the search ends without reaching one, report that no augmenting path exists.

**Correctness.** A directed path from an uncovered $x$ to an uncovered $y$ alternates between non-$M$ edges ($X\to Y$) and $M$-edges ($Y\to X$) and (as a BFS tree path) never repeats a vertex, so it is an augmenting path. Conversely, an augmenting path, written from its $X$-end $x$ to its $Y$-end $y$, follows exactly these directions, so $y$ is reachable from the uncovered vertex $x$ and the BFS finds it (BFS visits every vertex reachable from its sources). So the algorithm finds an augmenting path exactly when one exists. ∎

smt-2022-power-5-5b.title: Count visits
smt-2022-power-5-5b.body: Each vertex is marked visited the first time it is reached and is never processed again, so each vertex is dequeued at most once ($\le n$ steps). When a vertex is processed we scan its outgoing edges; each edge of $G$ appears as exactly one directed edge, so over the whole search each edge is scanned at most once ($\le m$ steps). Initialising the sources and building the path from parent pointers costs at most $n$ more. Hence the total time is at most $3(n+m)$, i.e. $c=3$ works (each membership test or list insertion takes time $1$). ∎

smt-2022-power-5-5c.title: Augment repeatedly
smt-2022-power-5-5c.body:
**Algorithm.** Start with $M=\emptyset$. Repeatedly run the augmenting-path search; if it returns a path, flip the edges along it (this enlarges $M$ by one and keeps it a matching, as in Berge's lemma); if it reports none, stop and output $M$.

**Correctness.** At termination there is no augmenting path, so $M$ is maximum by Berge's Lemma (Problem 5.4).

**Running time.** Each round increases $|M|$ by one and $|M|\le n/2$, so there are at most $n/2+1$ searches, each costing $O(n+m)$, plus flipping a path of length at most $n$. Total $O\left(n(n+m)\right)$. ∎

smt-2022-power-5-6.title: Cover argument
smt-2022-power-5-6.body: Since $M$ is maximal, every edge of $G$, in particular every edge of $M'$, has at least one endpoint covered by $M$ (otherwise it could be added to $M$). The edges of $M'$ are disjoint, so distinct edges of $M'$ use distinct covered vertices. There are only $|V(M)|=2|M|$ covered vertices, so $|M'|\le2|M|$, i.e. $|M|\ge\frac12|M'|$. ∎

smt-2022-power-6-1a.title: Greedy is maximal
smt-2022-power-6-1a.body:
**Algorithm.** When $x$ arrives, match it to an arbitrary neighbour in $Y$ that is still unmatched, if there is one.

**Analysis.** The resulting matching $M$ is maximal: suppose an edge $(x,y)$ could still be added at the end, i.e. both $x,y$ are unmatched. When $x$ arrived $y$ was unmatched (a matched vertex stays matched) and was a neighbour of $x$, so the algorithm would have matched $x$ to some free neighbour, contradicting that $x$ stays unmatched. By Problem 5.6, a maximal matching has at least half the size of a maximum matching, so $\mathrm{ALG}\ge\frac12|M^*|$ on every input, and the competitive ratio is at least $\frac12$. ∎

smt-2022-power-6-1b.title: Adversary argument
smt-2022-power-6-1b.body:
Let $Y=\{y_1,y_2\}$ and let $x_1$ arrive adjacent to both. A deterministic algorithm makes a decision about $x_1$ that depends only on this information.

- If it matches $x_1$ to $y_i$, let $x_2$ arrive adjacent only to $y_i$. Then $x_2$ cannot be matched, so $\mathrm{ALG}=1$, but the maximum matching $\{x_1y_{3-i},x_2y_i\}$ has size $2$: performance $\frac12$.
- If it leaves $x_1$ unmatched, the input ends there: $\mathrm{ALG}=0$ while the maximum matching has size $1$: performance $0$.

In every case the performance is at most $\frac12$, so the competitive ratio of any deterministic algorithm is at most $\frac12$. ∎

smt-2022-power-6-2.title: Marginal probabilities
smt-2022-power-6-2.body:
Define $m_{xy}=P[x\text{ is matched to }y\text{ by }\mathrm{ALG}]$. When $x$ arrives, these probabilities are determined by the history of the (known) distribution of $\mathrm{ALG}$ and the graph seen so far, so $\mathrm{FracALG}$ can compute and fix them deterministically at that time: it is an online deterministic fractional algorithm.

Feasibility: $\sum_ym_{xy}=P[x\text{ is matched}]\le1$ and $\sum_xm_{xy}=P[y\text{ is matched}]\le1$.

Let $w_{xy}$ be the indicator that $x$ is matched to $y$. By linearity of expectation, $\mathbb E[\mathrm{ALG}(G,L)]=\mathbb E\left[\sum_{(x,y)\in E}w_{xy}\right]=\sum_{(x,y)\in E}\mathbb E[w_{xy}]=\sum_{(x,y)\in E}m_{xy}$.

Conversely, given a deterministic fractional algorithm, when $x$ arrives choose a neighbour $y$ with probability $m_{xy}$ (the increment assigned to $x$), and leave $x$ unmatched with the remaining probability; the marginals equal $m_{xy}$ and the expected size is $\sum m_{xy}$ — a randomized integral algorithm (the load constraints give valid probabilities; dependence between choices is arranged by conditioning on the vertices already matched). ∎

smt-2022-power-6-3.title: Compare with $M^*$
smt-2022-power-6-3.body: The edges of $M^*$ are disjoint, so each vertex appears in at most one of them and $$\sum_{(x,y)\in M^*}(a_x+b_y)\le\sum_xa_x+\sum_yb_y,$$ because $a_x,b_y\ge0$ and the left side counts a subset of the terms. Each edge of $M^*$ has $a_x+b_y\ge c$, so the left side is at least $c|M^*|$. Therefore $\sum_{(x,y)\in E}m_{xy}=\sum_xa_x+\sum_yb_y\ge c|M^*|$. ∎

smt-2022-power-6-4b.title: Money of $x$
smt-2022-power-6-4b.body:
**Case $W^f_y=1$.** Then $b_y=G(1)-G(0)$, and the bound reads $a_x+b_y\ge G(1)-G(0)+1-g(1)$; this holds for the function $g$ chosen in part (c), which has $g(1)=1$ (and for general $g$ part (a) is the relevant bound).

**Case $W^f_y<1$.** Then $b_y=\int_0^{W_y^f}g=G(W^f_y)-G(0)$. Since $y\in N(x)$ never reached load $1$, when $x$ arrived the algorithm could not run out of neighbours with load below $1$, so $x$ spent its entire budget $1$: $\sum_{y'}m_{xy'}=1$. Every unit of that budget was put on a neighbour of lowest current load, and the load of $y$ at that time was at most $W^f_y$ (loads never decrease), so the receiving neighbour had load $\le W^f_y$ and $x$ collected at least $1-g(W^f_y)$ per unit ($1-g$ is decreasing since $g$ is increasing). Hence $a_x\ge1-g(W^f_y)$ and $a_x+b_y\ge G(W^f_y)-G(0)+1-g(W^f_y)$. ∎

smt-2022-power-6-4c.title: Solve the differential equation
smt-2022-power-6-4c.body: Differentiate $G(z)-G(0)+1-g(z)=c$: $g(z)-g'(z)=0$, so $g(z)=ke^z$ and we may take $G(z)=ke^z$. The condition at $z=0$: $0+1-g(0)=1-k=c$. The condition $G(1)-G(0)=k(e-1)=c$. So $k(e-1)=1-k$, i.e. $k=\frac1e$ and $c=1-\frac1e$. Thus $g(z)=e^{z-1}$, which is increasing with values in $[\frac1e,1]\subseteq[0,1]$ as required. The Water Level algorithm is therefore $\left(1-\frac1e\right)$-competitive. ∎

smt-2022-power-6-5a.title: Perfect matching
smt-2022-power-6-5a.body: $(i,i)\in E$ for each $i$, and these $n$ edges are disjoint, so there is a matching of size $n$; no matching can have more than $|X|=n$ edges. ∎

smt-2022-power-6-5b.title: Track the loads
smt-2022-power-6-5b.body:
All neighbours of $x=1$ ($y=1,\dots,n$) start at load $0$, so $x=1$ adds $\frac1n$ to each. For $x=2$ the neighbours $\{2,\dots,n\}$ all have load $\frac1n$, so each gets $\frac1{n-1}$, and so on: $x=t$ adds $\frac1{n-t+1}$ to every $y\ge t$ (they all have equal loads), as long as this does not push the loads above $1$. After $i$ arrivals, every $y\ge i$ has load $\sum_{t=1}^{i}\frac{1}{n-t+1}=H_n-H_{n-i}$.

The loads reach $1$ when $H_n-H_{n-i}\ge1$. By $H_n=\ln n+\gamma+o(1)$ this is $\ln\frac n{n-i}\approx1$, i.e. $i^*=n\left(1-\frac1e\right)+o(n)$. Each $x\le i^*$ gets its full budget $1$. For $x>i^*$ all neighbours $y\ge x>i^*$ already have load $1$, so $x$ receives nothing. Therefore Water Level produces a fractional matching of total value $i^*=n\left(1-\frac1e\right)+o(n)$, while the maximum matching has size $n$. The performance tends to $1-\frac1e$ as $n\to\infty$. ∎

smt-2022-power-6-5c.title: Union bound over the arrivals
smt-2022-power-6-5c.body:
Index the vertices of $Y$ by the time at which they are dropped from the neighbourhoods: let $y^{(j)}=S_j\setminus S_{j+1}$ (and $y^{(n)}=S_n$). Then $y^{(j)}$ is adjacent exactly to $x_1,\dots,x_j$.

When $x_i$ arrives the algorithm knows $S_i$ ($n-i+1$ vertices) but not which of them will be $y^{(i)},y^{(i+1)},\dots,y^{(n)}$: given everything the algorithm has seen, those labels are a uniformly random assignment of the elements of $S_i$. The algorithm (deterministic, or randomized by averaging over its random bits) matches $x_i$ to at most one element of $S_i$, so for every $j\ge i$, $P[x_i\text{ is matched to }y^{(j)}]\le\frac1{n-i+1}$.

Hence $P[y^{(j)}\text{ is matched}]\le\sum_{i=1}^jP[x_i\to y^{(j)}]\le\sum_{i=1}^j\frac1{n-i+1}$, and trivially it is at most $1$. Summing over $j$ and using linearity of expectation, $\mathbb E[\mathrm{ALG}]\le\sum_{j=1}^n\min\left(1,\sum_{i=1}^j\frac1{n-i+1}\right)$. A randomized algorithm is a distribution over deterministic ones, and the bound holds for each, so it holds for the average. ∎

smt-2022-power-6-5d.title: Averaging
smt-2022-power-6-5d.body: Choose $n$ large enough that the right-hand side is at most $1-\frac1e+\varepsilon$. By 6.5(c), the expected value of $\frac1n\mathrm{ALG}$ over the random ordering (and the algorithm's randomness) is at most this. An average of numbers is at least their minimum: if every ordering $L$ had $\frac1n\mathbb E[\mathrm{ALG}(G_n,L)]>1-\frac1e+\varepsilon$ then averaging over $L$ would give a larger value than the bound, a contradiction. So some fixed ordering $L_n$ has $\frac1n\mathbb E[\mathrm{ALG}(G_n,L_n)]\le1-\frac1e+\varepsilon$. Since the maximum matching has size $n$, the performance on $L_n$ is at most $1-\frac1e+\varepsilon$, and since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary no randomized integral algorithm has competitive ratio above $1-\frac1e$. (Together with the Water Level analysis this shows $1-\frac1e$ is optimal.) ∎

smt-2022-power-7-1a.title: Count proposals
smt-2022-power-7-1a.body: Each iteration of the loop is a proposal by some student $h$ to a school he has never proposed to before. Hence the number of iterations is at most the number of (student, school) pairs, $n\cdot n=n^2$, so the algorithm terminates. (Part (b) shows that an unmatched student always has a school left to propose to, so the loop cannot get stuck.) ∎

smt-2022-power-7-1b.title: Counting argument
smt-2022-power-7-1b.body: A school that has received a proposal stays matched from then on: it only ever switches to a better student, never to nobody. Suppose some student $h$ is unmatched but has already proposed to all $n$ schools. Then all $n$ schools are matched, to $n$ distinct students different from $h$, so there would be at least $n+1$ students, a contradiction. Hence every unmatched student still has a school to propose to, the loop only ends when no student is unmatched, and by part (a) it does end. At the end all $n$ students are matched to distinct schools, so $|M|=n$. ∎

smt-2022-power-7-2.title: Monotonicity
smt-2022-power-7-2.body:
Key observations: a student proposes down his list $L_h$, and a school only changes partner to a better one (it accepts only a student it prefers to its current partner).

Suppose the output $M$ has an unstable pair $(h_1,s_2)$ with $(h_1,s_1),(h_2,s_2)\in M$, $s_2\succ s_1$ in $L_{h_1}$ and $h_1\succ h_2$ in $L_{s_2}$. Since $h_1$ proposes down his list and ends with $s_1$, he proposed to $s_2$ before $s_1$, and was rejected by $s_2$ (or later dropped by it). When $s_2$ rejected or dropped $h_1$, it held (or accepted) some student $h_3\succ h_1$ in $L_{s_2}$. Since schools only improve, the final partner $h_2$ of $s_2$ satisfies $h_2\succeq h_3\succ h_1$ in $L_{s_2}$, contradicting $h_1\succ h_2$. So there is no unstable pair. ∎

smt-2022-power-7-3.title: Two arguments
smt-2022-power-7-3.body:
Call a school $s$ *possible* for a student $h$ if some stable matching pairs them, so $\mathrm{best}(h)$ is the highest-ranked possible school.

**Student-optimal.** Claim: no student is ever rejected by a school that is possible for him. Suppose otherwise and consider the first time a student $h$ is rejected (refused, or dropped later) by a possible school $s$. At that moment $s$ holds a student $h'$ with $h'\succ h$ in $L_s$. Let $M'$ be a stable matching containing $(h,s)$, and let $(h',s')\in M'$, so $s'\ne s$ is possible for $h'$. Student $h'$ is currently held by $s$; if he had proposed to $s'$ earlier, he would have left $s'$ only by being rejected by $s'$, a possible school for him, earlier than the present moment, contradicting the choice of the first rejection. So $h'$ has not proposed to $s'$ yet, although he proposed to $s$; since students propose down their lists, $s\succ s'$ in $L_{h'}$. Together with $h'\succ h$ in $L_s$ this makes $(h',s)$ an unstable pair of $M'$, a contradiction. Hence nobody is rejected by a possible school. A student $h$ proposes down his list and is never rejected by $\mathrm{best}(h)$, so the output matches him to $\mathrm{best}(h)$ or to a school ranked higher; but the output is stable (Problem 7.2), so its school is possible for $h$, hence equals $\mathrm{best}(h)$.

**School-pessimal.** Let $(h,s)$ be in the output $M$. Suppose some stable matching $M'$ gives $s$ a student $h''$ with $h\succ h''$ in $L_s$. In $M'$ the student $h$ is matched to some $s'\ne s$. By student-optimality $s=\mathrm{best}(h)$, so $s\succ s'$ in $L_h$. Then $(h,s)$ is an unstable pair of $M'$ ($h$ prefers $s$ to $s'$, and $s$ prefers $h$ to its partner $h''$), a contradiction. So no stable matching gives $s$ a worse partner than $h$; since $M$ itself is stable, $h=\mathrm{worst}(s)$. ∎

smt-2022-power-7-4.title: Two runs
smt-2022-power-7-4.body:
Let $M_H$ be the output of the proposal algorithm with students proposing (student-optimal and school-pessimal, Problem 7.3) and $M_S$ the output with the roles swapped, schools proposing (by the same theorem with roles exchanged it is school-optimal and student-pessimal: each student receives his worst stable partner).

If $(h,s)$ are soulmates they are matched in every stable matching, in particular in both $M_H$ and $M_S$. Conversely, suppose $(h,s)\in M_H\cap M_S$. Then $s=\mathrm{best}(h)$ because $M_H$ is student-optimal, and $s$ is also the *worst* stable partner of $h$ because $M_S$ is student-pessimal. So all of $h$'s stable partners lie between $s$ and $s$: $h$ has the same partner $s$ in every stable matching, i.e. they are soulmates.

**Algorithm.** Compute $M_H$ and $M_S$ by running the proposal algorithm twice (swapping the roles of students and schools). Output any pair in $M_H\cap M_S$; if the intersection is empty, there are no soulmates. ∎

smt-2022-power-7-5.title: Reduction to one-to-one
smt-2022-power-7-5.body:
Replace each school $s$ by $m$ copies $s_1,\dots,s_m$, each with a single spot and with the same ranking $L_s$ of the students. In every student's list replace $s$ by $s_1\succ s_2\succ\dots\succ s_m$ (consecutively, in that order, at the position of $s$). Now there are $mn$ students and $mn$ copies, so by Theorem 7.1 (proposal algorithm) there is a stable matching $M$ of the one-to-one problem. Assign student $h$ to school $s$ if $(h,s_i)\in M$ for some $i$; each school receives exactly $m$ students.

Suppose the assignment has an unstable pair $(h,s)$: $h$ is assigned to $s'\ne s$ via copy $s'_k$ (i.e. $(h,s'_k)\in M$), $s\succ s'$ in $L_h$, and $h\succ h'$ in $L_s$ for some $h'$ assigned to $s$, say $(h',s_j)\in M$. In $h$'s modified list every copy of $s$ is above every copy of $s'$, so $s_j\succ s'_k$ in $L_h$; and in $L_{s_j}=L_s$, $h\succ h'$. Hence $(h,s_j)$ is an unstable pair of $M$, contradicting stability. So the assignment is stable. ∎
